answers.stem_only: Convert the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment: a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover keeps writes going without losing committed data. The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance serves no reads, so the reporting detail is a distractor; the application keeps using the same endpoint.

Use point-in-time recovery from the automated backups to a time 5 minutes before the deletion. RDS restores to a NEW DB instance (no in-place rollback for RDS for MySQL); then copy the table back to production and delete the temporary instance. The Multi-AZ standby replicated the deletion too.

Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance and point the application at the proxy endpoint. The proxy holds client connections, routes to the new primary after failover without waiting for DNS propagation, and shortens failover time; only a configuration change is needed.
A read replica requires automated backups on the source. A backup retention period of 0 turns them off, so set the retention period to a value greater than 0 first, then create the replica.

Create a read replica (asynchronous replication) and send the reporting queries to the replica endpoint, which offloads reads from the primary. A Multi-AZ DB instance standby cannot serve reads, and self-managed EC2 adds overhead.

Two layers must survive an AZ failure: the web tier (Auto Scaling group across at least two AZs behind an Application Load Balancer) and the database (Multi-AZ deployment with a synchronous standby and automatic failover).

Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment (one writer, two readable standbys in three AZs): failover typically under a minute, plus a reader endpoint that serves read-only queries from the standbys. A Multi-AZ DB instance standby is not readable.

Automated backups expire with the retention period (at most 35 days), so take a manual DB snapshot now; manual snapshots stay until someone deletes them, which covers 7 years. (AWS Backup with a 7-year rule would also work, if offered.)

Move to Provisioned IOPS SSD storage, specifically io2 Block Express, which gives consistent sub-millisecond latency for I/O-intensive OLTP, and provision the IOPS for peak. Instance class, gp2 size or storage autoscaling do not fix storage latency.

Use Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments: RDS creates a green copy kept in sync by logical replication, you upgrade and test the green environment, then switch over, usually in about a minute. An in-place Multi-AZ upgrade upgrades both primary and standby together and causes downtime.

Stop the DB instance outside working hours and start it each working morning on an automated schedule (for example EventBridge Scheduler or Instance Scheduler on AWS). A stopped instance keeps its data and you pay only for storage; daily stops stay well inside the 7-day auto-start limit.

Change nothing: the application already pools a small, steady number of long-lived connections far below the limit, so RDS Proxy adds cost and a network hop (extra latency) with no benefit. Keep the direct connection.
Too many connections at low CPU from many short-lived Lambda invocations is the classic RDS Proxy case: the proxy pools and shares connections. Only the connection endpoint changes, not the SQL.

Encryption cannot be turned on for an existing unencrypted DB instance, and an encrypted read replica cannot be made from an unencrypted source. Take a snapshot, copy it with encryption under the KMS key, restore a new encrypted DB instance from the copy, and cut over; its backups and replicas are then encrypted.

Amazon RDS Custom for SQL Server: a managed database (automated backups and other automation) that still gives access to the host operating system so the vendor's agent can be installed. Standard RDS gives no OS access; EC2 is fully self-managed.

Create a cross-Region read replica in us-west-2 (asynchronous, recovery point of seconds to minutes) and promote it in a disaster. KMS keys are Regional, so an encrypted cross-Region replica must use a KMS key in the destination Region us-west-2.

Automated snapshots cannot be shared, and snapshots encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/rds cannot be shared (its key policy cannot be changed). Copy the automated snapshot to a manual snapshot encrypted with a customer managed key, grant the backup account use of that key, and share the manual copy; the backup account copies it and can restore.

Low freeable memory with high and rising read IOPS means the working set no longer fits in memory and reads go to storage. Scale to a memory-optimized instance class (for example r-class) during the maintenance window. Connections are not the problem, so not RDS Proxy.
Turn on RDS storage autoscaling with a maximum storage threshold: RDS grows storage automatically when free space runs low, and you pay only for what is allocated as it grows.

Create a final DB snapshot at deletion. It is a manual snapshot that stays until deleted, covering 2 years. Automated backups expire with the retention period (maximum 35 days), and a stopped instance restarts automatically after 7 days.

High CPU from read queries with few connections: offload the reads to a read replica and point the read-only connection settings at the replica endpoint. RDS Proxy fixes connection count, not CPU; a Multi-AZ DB instance standby serves no reads.

Choose RDS for MySQL (or MariaDB): its read replicas can be made writable by setting the read_only parameter to 0 in the replica's parameter group, so the team can add indexes and tables while replication continues. RDS for PostgreSQL read replicas are read-only.
